blocks.text: Order of the Articles (smallest number first): Art 352 is National Emergency, then Art 356 is President's Rule, then Art 358 suspends Article 19 during National Emergency, and last, Art 360 is Financial Emergency.
Do not confuse: Art 311 is about dismissal of civil servants. It has nothing to do with Financial Emergency (that is Art 360).

sections.heading: Why emergency provisions exist (federal becomes unitary)

items: Purpose: to let the Central government meet any abnormal situation effectively.
Reason for including them: to protect the sovereignty, unity, integrity and security of the country, the democratic political system and the Constitution.
During an emergency, the Centre becomes all-powerful and the States come under the total control of the Centre.
So the federal structure changes into a unitary one WITHOUT any formal amendment of the Constitution. No amendment and no ratification by States is needed.
This change (federal in normal times, unitary in emergency) is called a UNIQUE feature of the Indian Constitution. It is NOT a borrowed feature.

Emergency provisions are a unitary (non-federal) feature of the Constitution. Example: when the President takes over a State's administration, this goes against the principle of federalism (sharing of power between Centre and States).
What India borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany: the provision to suspend Fundamental Rights during an emergency.

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
Remark
rows: Said the Indian Constitution can be both unitary and federal, as time and circumstances need. It is federal in normal times but works as though it were unitary in an emergency. The American federal system cannot change like this.

sections.heading: Article 355 and the Emergency Articles list

blocks.title: Article 355 — two duties of the Union (Centre)
items: To protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance.
To make sure the government of every State is carried on as per the provisions of the Constitution.
To carry out this second duty, the Centre takes over a State's government under Art 356 (President's Rule). So Art 355 explains why Art 356 exists.

blocks.text: Related Articles outside this Part: Art 263 is the Inter-State Council. Art 201 is about Bills reserved by the Governor for the President's consideration. Art 365 is about a State failing to follow the Union's directions (see President's Rule).

blocks.title: Critics
head: Member
What he said
rows: Feared this chapter would lay the foundation of 'a totalitarian state, a police state' (a state ruled by force, with no freedom).
Called it 'a chapter of reaction and retrogression' (going backwards).
Feared the President and the Executive would exercise 'a form of constitutional dictatorship' (one-person rule made legal by the Constitution).
Said the financial emergency provisions are 'a serious threat to the financial autonomy of the States'.

blocks.title: Supporters
head: Member
What he said
rows: Called them 'the very life-breath of the Constitution'.
Said they would work as a 'safety-valve' (releasing pressure in a crisis) and help maintain the Constitution.
Defended them, but accepted they could be misused for political purposes. Hoped Art 356 would remain a 'dead-letter' (a law that is never used), used only as a last resort.

blocks.title: Main grounds of criticism
items: Federal character would be destroyed; the Union would become all-powerful.
All power would be concentrated in the Union executive.
The President would become a dictator.
Financial autonomy (freedom to manage their own money) of the States would be destroyed.
Fundamental Rights would become meaningless.

head: Change
Before
After 44th Amendment (1978)

President can proclaim only after the Union Cabinet's decision is given to him in writing
The right to move courts for Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended
Only if (1) a National Emergency is in force, AND (2) the Election Commission certifies that it is difficult to hold elections

blocks.text: The 44th Amendment did NOT remove Fundamental Duties (Art 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment). They are still in the Constitution.
see National Emergency for all 44th Amendment changes

items: Emergency is in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360). Do not confuse: Part XI is Centre–State relations, and Part XX is amendment of the Constitution.
The Constitution says 'proclamation of emergency', never 'National Emergency'. For President's Rule, it does not use the word 'emergency' at all.
The change from federal to unitary happens WITHOUT any amendment. This is a unique feature, not a borrowed one.
From the Weimar Constitution of Germany, India borrowed only one thing: suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency.
Parliament's approval: National Emergency within 1 month, by special majority. President's Rule and Financial Emergency within 2 months, by simple majority.
To disapprove (end) a National Emergency: Lok Sabha alone can do it, by simple majority.
Financial Emergency: no maximum period, no repeated approval needed, and never used so far.
Art 355 is the duty of the Union to protect States. Art 356 is President's Rule. Art 365 (failure to follow Union directions) is NOT the duty Article.

subcards.title: National Emergency (Art 352)
subcards.summary: When and how a National Emergency is declared, and what it changes.
at_a_glance: Art 352 (Part XVIII). The Constitution calls it a 'Proclamation of Emergency'
War, external aggression (attack from outside) or armed rebellion — or imminent danger of these
President, only after the Union Cabinet's decision is sent to him in writing (44th Amendment, 1978)
Both Houses of Parliament, within 1 month, by special majority
6 months at a time; can be renewed any number of times, each time with Parliament's approval
President at any time; must revoke if Lok Sabha passes a disapproval resolution by simple majority
Art 19 suspended automatically (only in war or external aggression); Art 20 and Art 21 can never be suspended

blocks.title: Grounds under Art 352
head: Ground
Popular name
Note
rows: External aggression (attack by a foreign country)
1962 and 1971 Emergencies were on this ground
Added by the 44th Amendment (1978) in place of 'internal disturbance'
Removed in 1978 because it was too vague. The 1975 Emergency was on this ground. Today NO Emergency can be declared on this ground.
blocks.note: Emergency can be declared even BEFORE the war, aggression or rebellion actually happens, if the President is satisfied there is imminent danger (danger that is about to happen).

blocks.title: Key rules about the proclamation
items: Advice: the President can declare it only when the Union Cabinet's decision is communicated to him in writing — not on the Prime Minister's advice alone. Added by the 44th Amendment (1978).
Why this safeguard: in 1975 Prime Minister Indira Gandhi advised the President without consulting her Cabinet; the Cabinet was told only after the proclamation was made.

'Cabinet' meaning: Art 352 defines the Cabinet as the Prime Minister and other ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Art 75. Art 352 is the only Article where the word 'Cabinet' appears in the Constitution.
Whole or part: an Emergency may cover all of India or only a part. The 42nd Amendment (1976) allowed the President to limit it to a specified part.

More than one: the President can issue different proclamations on different grounds even while one is already in force. Added by the 38th Amendment (1975). Example: the 1975 Emergency was declared while the 1971 Emergency was still in force.

Do not mix up two rules. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the President bound, in general, by the advice of the Council of Ministers (Art 74). This is true, but it is NOT the reason for the Art 352 rule. The written-Cabinet-decision rule for Emergency came separately, from the 44th Amendment (1978).

blocks.title: If Lok Sabha is dissolved
items: If Lok Sabha is dissolved when the Emergency is declared (or is dissolved within the 1 month without approving it), the proclamation survives until 30 days from the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha — provided the Rajya Sabha has approved it in the meantime.
If the new Lok Sabha does not approve it within those 30 days, it ends.
The same rule applies to a renewal when Lok Sabha is dissolved during the 6-month period.

blocks.text: During a National Emergency the Centre becomes all-powerful and the federal system works like a unitary one (one strong central government), without any formal amendment of the Constitution. State governments and State legislatures are NOT suspended — they keep working, but under the Centre's control.

blocks.title: Three effects
head: Area
What happens
Article
rows: The Centre can give directions to any State on ANY matter (in normal times, only on certain specified matters). State governments are controlled but not suspended.
Parliament can make laws on any subject in the State List, for the whole or any part of India. The State legislature's power is not suspended, but Parliament's law overrides it.
Laws made by Parliament on State subjects become inoperative (stop working) six months after the Emergency ends.
If Parliament is not in session, the President can issue ordinances (temporary laws made by the President) on State List subjects too.
Parliament can give powers and duties to the Centre and its officers on matters outside the Union List, to carry out its Emergency laws.
The executive and legislative effects extend not only to the State where Emergency is in operation but also to any other State (42nd Amendment, 1976).

The President can modify the distribution of revenues between Centre and States — that is, REDUCE or CANCEL transfers of money from Centre to States (not increase). This lasts till the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends. Every such order must be laid before both Houses of Parliament.

blocks.title: Two different routes for Parliament to make State List laws
head: Aspect
National Emergency (Art 250)
President's Rule (Art 356, Art 357)

Parliament, while the State legislature also continues
Parliament, or the President or another authority named by Parliament, because the State legislature is suspended or dissolved
Law stops working 6 months after the Emergency ends
Law continues until the State legislature changes or repeals it
Only the State under President's Rule

blocks.title: Do not confuse with Art 249
items: Under Art 249 (normal times), the Rajya Sabha alone can pass a resolution, supported by two-thirds of members present and voting, saying Parliament should make a law on a State List matter in the national interest. This needs no Emergency.

sections.heading: Effect on Fundamental Rights (Art 358 and Art 359)

blocks.title: Article 358 — Art 19 freedoms
head: Point
Rule
rows: The six freedoms of Art 19 are suspended AUTOMATICALLY when Emergency is declared. No separate order is needed.
Only war or external aggression (External Emergency) — NOT armed rebellion. Limit added by the 44th Amendment (1978).
The State can make laws or take executive action that cut down Art 19 rights; they cannot be challenged for violating Art 19.

Only a law that contains a recital (a statement in the law itself) that it relates to the Emergency is protected — Art 358(2). The date of making the law alone is not enough. Executive action (an order or act of the government) is protected only if taken under such a law. This condition was added by the 44th Amendment (1978).
Emergency in only part of India

Protection can also cover a law or action in another part of India, if and to the extent the security of India is threatened by activities in or related to the Emergency area (proviso to Art 358(1)). The other conditions still apply.
Art 19 revives automatically. Emergency laws stop working to the extent they violate Art 19. But no remedy lies for things done during the Emergency — they cannot be challenged even later.

blocks.title: Article 359 — enforcement of other rights
head: Point
Rule
rows: The President by ORDER suspends the right to move any court to enforce the Fundamental Rights named in the order. The rights themselves are not suspended — only their enforcement (going to court).
Includes the High Court (Art 226) as well as the Supreme Court (Art 32). Going to the High Court instead does not avoid the suspension.
Art 20 (protection in respect of conviction for offences) and Art 21 (right to life and personal liberty). Added by the 44th Amendment (1978).
For the whole Emergency or a shorter period; for the whole of India or any part.
Every order must be laid before each House of Parliament.

Art 359(1A) protects laws that limit the rights named in the President's order. But under Art 359(1B), this protection applies only to a law that contains a recital (a statement in the law itself) that it relates to the Emergency. Executive action not taken under such a law is also NOT protected.
Laws stop working to the extent of inconsistency when the ORDER ends — even if the Emergency continues. Things done during the order still cannot be challenged.

blocks.title: Art 358 vs Art 359
head: Aspect
Art 358
Art 359
rows: Rights named in the President's order
Whole duration or shorter, as in the order
Protects only Emergency-related laws and action under them

blocks.title: Key points
items: So during Emergency some Fundamental Rights can be suspended, except Art 20 and Art 21. Fundamental Rights are in Part III (not Part IV), are enforceable in court, and are not absolute. Some are available only to citizens, others to all persons, including foreigners.
A person detained without any law during an External Emergency can still go to court to enforce Art 21.
The idea of suspending Fundamental Rights during Emergency was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

Martial law (Art 34) is different: Parliament can, by law, indemnify (protect from legal action) officials for acts done to restore order in a martial-law area. It is not automatic. Art 34 does not contain the Art 352 proclamation procedure. Martial law affects only Fundamental Rights; National Emergency also affects Centre–State relations and Lok Sabha's term.

blocks.title: Judicial review of the proclamation
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Made the declaration of National Emergency immune from judicial review (courts could not examine it). It also did the same for the President's satisfaction under Art 356 and Art 360.
Deleted this immunity for all three — Art 352, Art 356 and Art 360. Courts can examine the President's decision again.

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Indira Nehru Gandhi vs. Raj Narain (1975)

Background: the Allahabad High Court had set aside Indira Gandhi's 1971 election in June 1975. In the Supreme Court appeal, the Court struck down Art 329A(4), added by the 39th Amendment, because it violated the basic structure (core features of the Constitution that Parliament cannot amend away).
The Allahabad High Court verdict triggered the 1975 Emergency.

Habeas Corpus case: while a President's order under Art 359 suspended enforcement of Art 21, a detenu (detained person) could not move a High Court for habeas corpus (a writ asking the court to examine whether a detention is legal). Upheld Section 16A(9) of MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act), 1971, the detention law of that time. Only dissent: Justice H.R. Khanna.
Shows why the 44th Amendment made Art 20 and Art 21 non-suspendable. Expressly overruled by a nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India (2017).
A proclamation of National Emergency can be challenged if it is malafide (in bad faith), or based on wholly extraneous and irrelevant facts, or is absurd or perverse.
Courts can review an Emergency proclamation.

items: MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was passed in 1971 when Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister; it was repealed in 1978.

President

items: 'Internal disturbance' is NOT a ground today; 'armed rebellion' replaced it (44th Amendment, 1978).
Approval: within 1 month, special majority, BOTH Houses. Disapproval: Lok Sabha ALONE, simple majority; notice by one-tenth of Lok Sabha members, and a special sitting within 14 days.
No maximum period for National Emergency (renewal every 6 months); President's Rule maximum is 3 years.
State legislatures and governments are NOT suspended in National Emergency. They can be suspended only under President's Rule.

The President can reduce or cancel money transfers to States — not increase them. Lok Sabha's term is extended by Parliament by law, not by the President.
Art 358 works only in war or external aggression, and it is automatic. Art 359 needs a President's order, and that order can never cover Art 20 and Art 21.
'Constitutional Emergency' (in Laxmikanth) is another name for President's Rule (Art 356), not National Emergency.

subcards.title: President's Rule (Art 356, 365)
subcards.summary: When and how the Centre takes over a State's government, and its limits.
at_a_glance: By both Houses of Parliament, within 2 months, by simple majority
6 months at a time; maximum 3 years in total
Needs BOTH a National Emergency AND an Election Commission certificate (44th Amendment)

sections.heading: What President's Rule is and when it can be imposed

blocks.text: When the government of a State cannot run according to the Constitution, the Centre (Union Government) takes over that State's government. This is called President's Rule. It is also called 'State Emergency' or 'Constitutional Emergency'. But the Constitution itself does not use the word 'emergency' for it.

blocks.title: Articles you must know
head: Article
What it says
rows: Duty of the Union (Centre) to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance, and to make sure every State government runs according to the Constitution. President's Rule is imposed in performance of this duty.
President's Rule itself — 'failure of constitutional machinery in States'. It is the most controversial and most criticised Article of the Constitution.
How the State's law-making powers are used while President's Rule is on. Parliament can hand this power over to the President.
If a State does not obey (comply with) directions given by the Centre, the President may treat this as a failure of constitutional machinery — so President's Rule can follow.

States must use their executive power so that Parliament's laws are obeyed and the Centre's executive power is not blocked. The Centre can give directions to States for this — for example, under Art 257, on building and maintaining means of communication (roads, waterways and the like) declared to be of national or military importance. Art 256 to Art 263 in Part XI deal with these administrative relations. Art 365 is the 'punishment' (coercive sanction) behind these directions, so they are binding, not mere advice.

blocks.title: Two grounds for President's Rule
head: Ground
Where
Explanation
rows: 1. Government of the State cannot be carried on according to the Constitution
The President acts on the Governor's report, OR 'otherwise' — that is, even without any report from the Governor.
2. State fails to obey Union directions
The President may hold that the State's constitutional machinery has failed.

blocks.title: Who does what
items: The Governor of the State sends the report to the President (Art 356(1) refers to this report). The Governor is the authority who recommends dismissal of the State government and suspension or dissolution of the Assembly.
The President decides, on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers. The President can also act without any Governor's report.

The Chief Minister can advise the Governor to dissolve the State Assembly, just as the Prime Minister can advise dissolution of the Lok Sabha. But a Chief Minister has no role in recommending President's Rule.
Art 356 was modelled on Section 93 of the Government of India Act, 1935 (the British-era provision that let the Governor take over a province's government).

sections.heading: Approval by Parliament, duration and revocation

blocks.title: Life of a President's Rule proclamation

steps.detail: Based on the Governor's report or otherwise.

steps.step: Both Houses of Parliament must approve it within TWO months
steps.detail: By simple majority (majority of members present and voting) in each House. If the Lok Sabha is dissolved at that time, the proclamation survives until 30 days after the new Lok Sabha's first sitting, provided the Rajya Sabha has approved it meanwhile.

steps.step: Once approved, it lasts SIX months
steps.detail: It can be extended by Parliament every six months.
After that it must end and normal constitutional government must return.

steps.step: Beyond ONE year — only if BOTH conditions are met (44th Amendment, 1978)
steps.detail: (1) A National Emergency is in operation in the whole of India or in the whole or any part of that State, AND (2) the Election Commission certifies that elections to that State Assembly cannot be held because of difficulties.
The President can revoke it at any time by a later proclamation. This needs no approval of Parliament. The Lok Sabha has NO power to force its revocation (unlike National Emergency).

blocks.title: Amendments on duration and review (in order)
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Made the President's satisfaction under Art 356 'final and conclusive' — it could not be questioned in any court.
Raised the period of each approval from six months to one year.

Brought the period back to six months. Added the two conditions for going beyond one year. Removed the 38th Amendment's bar on courts, so the President's satisfaction CAN be checked by courts (judicial review) — for Art 352, Art 356 and Art 360 alike.
A special amendment that allowed President's Rule imposed in Punjab in May 1987 to continue for five years — beyond the normal three-year limit.

blocks.title: Time limits — quick match
head: Item
Time
rows: Each renewal of National Emergency or President's Rule
No limit; once approved, no repeated approval needed

blocks.title: Majority needed in Parliament
head: Resolution
Majority
rows: Special majority in both Houses (majority of total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting)
Simple majority in the Lok Sabha only

blocks.text: Rajya Sabha note: approval and each extension of President's Rule needs resolutions of BOTH Houses; the Rajya Sabha has no special or extra power here. A different Rajya Sabha power: under Art 249, a Rajya Sabha resolution letting Parliament make laws on a State List subject is valid for one year.

blocks.title: Powers the President gets
items: Takes over the functions of the State government and the powers of the Governor or any other State executive authority.
Declares that the State Legislature's powers will be exercised by Parliament, or under Parliament's authority.
Can take all other necessary steps, including suspending the constitutional provisions about any body or authority in the State (but NOT the High Court).

blocks.title: In practice
items: The State Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister is dismissed.
The Governor runs the State on the President's behalf, with the Chief Secretary or advisers appointed by the President.

The State Assembly is either suspended or dissolved. 'Suspended' (also called 'suspended animation') means the Assembly is kept alive but does not meet, so it can be revived later. Dissolution is NOT automatic. If it is dissolved, fresh elections are held.
Parliament passes the State's bills and the State budget.

blocks.title: Law-making under Art 357 (when the Assembly is suspended or dissolved)
head: Rule
Detail
rows: Parliament can hand over the power to make laws for the State to the President, or to any authority the President names. In practice the President makes these laws after consulting the Members of Parliament from that State. These laws are called 'President's Acts'.
When the Lok Sabha is not in session, the President can authorise spending from the State's Consolidated Fund until Parliament sanctions it.
Laws continue after President's Rule ends
Such laws do NOT lapse. They stay in force until the State Legislature changes, repeals or re-enacts them.

blocks.title: What does NOT change
items: The State High Court: the President cannot take over its powers or suspend provisions about it. Its status, powers and functions stay the same.
Fundamental Rights: President's Rule has no effect on them. Art 19 (freedoms of speech, movement and so on) is NOT suspended.
Other States: only the State under President's Rule has its relationship with the Centre changed.
Local bodies (panchayats, municipalities) are not dissolved because of President's Rule.

President takes over the functions of that State's government; State legislature's powers used by or under Parliament
Centre can direct States to follow canons (rules) of financial propriety, and to cut salaries of State employees
Not an emergency itself: it is the Union's duty to protect States from external aggression and internal disturbance

head: Article
Subject
rows: Distribution of revenues while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation
Duty of the Union to protect States
Legislative powers under a proclamation issued under Art 356
Suspension of Art 19 during an Emergency

blocks.text: see National Emergency (Art 352)

items.detail: President's Rule was imposed for the first time in Punjab (20 June 1951). In exam options, PEPSU and Kerala are wrong.
On 31 July 1959 the elected Communist government of E.M.S. Namboodiripad was dismissed under Art 356, even though it still had a majority in the Assembly.

items.what: Janata Government dismissed 9 Congress State governments
items.detail: The ground given: after Congress lost the Lok Sabha elections, those State Assemblies no longer reflected the people's wishes. The 9 States: Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal and Haryana.

items.what: Congress returned and did the same in 9 States
items.detail: The 9 States: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Orissa, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.
President's Rule imposed in May 1987 ran for about five years. This was possible only because the 68th Amendment (1991) allowed it to go beyond the normal three-year limit.

President's Rule in Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan — because these governments did not sincerely implement the Centre's ban on certain religious organisations (after the Babri Masjid demolition). The S.R. Bommai case (1994) upheld these three.

items: Laxmikanth: President's Rule has been imposed more than 125 times since 1950, often arbitrarily, for political or personal reasons. Recent counts on the web put it at about 134 times (as of Nov 2026).
Almost all States have been under President's Rule at least once.

blocks.title: Who said what about Art 356 and emergency powers
head: Person
Said
rows: Hoped Art 356 would remain a 'dead letter' and be used only as a last resort. He also admitted the Articles could be abused for political purposes.
Mocked Ambedkar's hope: 'Dr. Ambedkar is dead and the Articles are very much alive.' He also feared the emergency chapter would lay the foundation of a 'totalitarian state, a police state'.
Called the emergency chapter 'a chapter of reaction and retrogression'.
Said the Financial Emergency provisions threaten the financial independence (autonomy) of States.
Supported the emergency provisions: called them 'the very life-breath of the Constitution'.
Supported the emergency provisions: called them a 'safety-valve'.
blocks.note: Critics say the 'dead letter' became a 'deadly weapon' against State governments.

sections.heading: Judicial review and the S.R. Bommai case

blocks.text: The 38th Amendment had stopped courts from questioning the President's decision; the 44th Amendment (1978) removed that bar. So courts can now check whether the President's satisfaction was proper (judicial review). The S.R. Bommai case (1994) is the landmark judgment on President's Rule. For a question asking which case first clearly held that President's Rule is open to judicial review, the answer is S.R. Bommai.

blocks.title: Principles laid down in S.R. Bommai case (1994)
head: No.
Principle
rows: The proclamation of President's Rule is subject to judicial review.

The President's satisfaction must be based on relevant material. The court can strike the proclamation down if it rests on irrelevant or outside (extraneous) grounds, or is mala fide (made in bad faith), or is perverse (one no reasonable person would reach).
The burden of proving that relevant material exists lies on the Centre.
The court cannot examine whether the material is correct or adequate (enough). It only checks whether the material is relevant.
If the proclamation is held invalid, the court can restore the dismissed government and revive the Assembly.
The Assembly should be dissolved only AFTER Parliament approves the proclamation. Until then it can only be suspended. If Parliament does not approve, the Assembly comes back to life.
Secularism is a 'basic feature' of the Constitution. A State government following anti-secular politics can face action under Art 356.
Whether a government has lost majority must be decided by a floor test (vote in the Assembly), not by the Governor's own opinion or letters from MLAs.
A new party coming to power at the Centre cannot dismiss State governments formed by other parties.
Art 356 is an exceptional power, to be used only occasionally.
Federalism is a basic feature of the Constitution. States are not 'mere appendages' (attached parts) of the Centre. Overriding State powers during an emergency is the EXCEPTION, not the rule.

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Upheld President's Rule in Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan (1992), on the ground of secularism. Did NOT uphold it in Nagaland (1988), Karnataka (1989) and Meghalaya (1991).
Gave the main guidelines on Art 356: floor test for majority, and judicial review of the proclamation.

The Supreme Court held that the 2005 dissolution of the Bihar Assembly under Art 356 was unconstitutional, because the Governor's report was not based on proper material. The Assembly was not restored, as fresh elections had already been held.
Shows the Bommai rules being applied to check a Governor's report.

blocks.title: Proper and improper use (Sarkaria Commission, accepted in Bommai)
head: Proper
Improper
rows: Hung Assembly — after elections, no party gets a majority
Ministry loses majority and the Governor recommends President's Rule without first checking whether another government can be formed
Majority party refuses to form a ministry and no coalition with majority can be found
Governor decides on majority by his own judgement, without a floor test (vote in the Assembly)
Ministry resigns after defeat and no one else can form a majority government
Ruling party, though it has a majority in the Assembly, suffers a big defeat in Lok Sabha elections (as used in 1977 and 1980)
State government ignores a constitutional direction of the Centre
Internal disturbance that does not amount to internal subversion or physical breakdown (see the 'Proper' column)
Internal subversion — the government deliberately acts against the Constitution or encourages violent revolt
Maladministration, corruption charges or severe financial difficulty
Physical breakdown — the government wilfully refuses to do its constitutional duties, endangering the State's security
No prior warning given to the State to correct itself (except in extreme urgency)
Used to settle the ruling party's internal problems, or for any irrelevant purpose

blocks.title: Sarkaria Commission (appointed 1983, report 1988; chairman R.S. Sarkaria)
head: Recommendation
Detail
rows: Only in extreme cases, as a last resort, when all other options have failed. It did NOT ask for deletion of Art 356.
Before imposing it, the Centre should warn the State in specific terms that it is not being run according to the Constitution (except in urgency).
Must be a 'speaking document' — that is, it must state the clear facts and reasons, not just a bare recommendation.
The Governor cannot dismiss a ministry so long as it has majority in the Assembly.
The five-year term should not be cut short except for extremely compelling reasons.
Should be an eminent person from outside the State, a detached figure not active in recent politics. (The Punchhi Commission later repeated this.)
The Centre can deploy armed forces without State consent, but States should preferably be consulted.
Should STAY with Parliament (not given to States). Other residuary powers go to the Concurrent List.
When the President withholds assent to a State bill, reasons should be told to the State.
Set up a permanent Inter-State Council under Art 263. It was set up in 1990.

blocks.title: Punchhi Commission (appointed 2007, report 2010; chairman M.M. Punchhi, former Chief Justice of India)
head: Recommendation
Detail
rows: Amend Art 355 and Art 356 so that only a troubled district, or part of a district, comes under Central rule — not the whole State. The State government and Assembly continue to work. Such a 'localised emergency' should not last more than THREE months.
Use Art 356 only as a last resort, strictly following the S.R. Bommai (1994) guidelines; amend the Constitution to include those guidelines. It did NOT ask for deletion of Art 356.
During communal violence the Centre may send its forces without the State's consent for a short period (about one week); beyond that, only with the State's consent.

The President should decide on a State bill reserved for him (Art 201) within six months. The Governor should decide within six months whether to give assent to a bill or reserve it for the President.
Fixed five-year term; removal only by impeachment by the State Legislature (like the President's impeachment). Governors should no longer be Chancellors of universities.
When inviting a leader to become Chief Minister, an alliance formed before the elections (pre-poll alliance) should be treated as one party.
Zonal Councils should meet at least twice a year; the National Integration Council at least once a year (NOT 'once in two years').

blocks.title: Demands to remove President's Rule
head: Body (year)
Demand
rows: Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu DMK government; report 1971)
Omit Art 356, Art 357 and Art 365 completely; abolish the All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS). The Centre completely ignored the report — it was NOT accepted in 1971.
The Centre's powers should be limited to defence, foreign affairs, communications and currency.

blocks.title: President's Rule in Andhra State and Andhra Pradesh
head: Spell
Period
Reason
rows: T. Prakasam ministry fell after losing its majority
United Andhra Pradesh — FIRST time in Andhra Pradesh
18 January 1973 – 10 December 1973 (about 11 months — the LONGEST of the three spells)
Law and order broke down during the Jai Andhra movement
Chief Minister (N. Kiran Kumar Reddy) and Congress MLAs resigned over the bill to bifurcate (divide) the State
blocks.note: Three spells in all: one in Andhra State and two in Andhra Pradesh. In time order: fall of the Prakasam ministry (1954), then the Jai Andhra movement (1973), then bifurcation (2014). Andhra Pradesh as a State was formed only in 1956, so 1973 is Andhra Pradesh's first President's Rule.

blocks.text: December 2020: the Andhra Pradesh High Court asked whether it could record a finding that 'constitutional machinery has broken down' in the State. The Constitution's provision for breakdown of constitutional machinery in a State is Art 356.

blocks.title: Recent instances (as of Nov 2026)
head: State
Period
Note
rows: Chief Minister N. Biren Singh resigned on 9 February 2025, amid ethnic violence going on since May 2023. The Assembly was kept suspended (not dissolved). Parliament extended it once, from August 2025. It was revoked on 4 February 2026, and Y. Khemchand Singh became Chief Minister the same day. This was Manipur's 11th spell of President's Rule — the most for any State.

items: As of Nov 2026 no State is under President's Rule.
Telangana and Chhattisgarh have never been under President's Rule (as of Nov 2026).

Approval: within TWO months, by simple majority, in both Houses. Maximum: THREE years. Going beyond ONE year needs BOTH a National Emergency AND an Election Commission certificate — not just one of them.

The Governor's report is NOT compulsory — the President can act 'otherwise'. President's Rule is imposed under Art 356. A State ignoring Union directions (Art 365) also leads to Art 356. It is never Art 352 or Art 360.
During President's Rule: the Assembly is NOT automatically dissolved; the High Court is NOT taken over; Fundamental Rights (including Art 19) are NOT suspended; local bodies are NOT dissolved.
Lok Sabha cannot force revocation of President's Rule — only the President revokes it.
Laws made during President's Rule continue until the State Legislature changes them. But laws made under Art 250 (during a National Emergency) end six months after the emergency ends.
44th Amendment removed the judicial-review bar for Art 352, 356 AND 360 — not only Art 352.
Sarkaria and Punchhi did NOT ask to delete Art 356. The Rajamannar Committee (Art 356, Art 357, Art 365) and the West Bengal Memorandum (Art 356, Art 357, Art 360) did.
First President's Rule in India: Punjab, 1951. Andhra Pradesh: its first and longest spell was in 1973 (Jai Andhra movement).

subcards.title: Financial Emergency (Art 360)
subcards.summary: When the money position (financial stability or credit) of India is in danger, the President can declare it and the Centre takes full control of state finances.
at_a_glance: Financial stability or credit of India, or of any part of India, is threatened
Both Houses of Parliament, within two months
Simple majority (majority of members present and voting)
No maximum period. Once Parliament approves it, no further approval is needed
Supreme Court and High Court judges' salaries can be reduced
Never declared — not even in the 1991 financial crisis

items: Article 360 lets the President proclaim a Financial Emergency if he or she is satisfied that the financial stability or credit of India, or of any part of its territory, is threatened.
'Credit' here means India's ability to borrow money and be trusted to repay it.

blocks.title: Can a court question the President's decision?

items.what: Made the President's satisfaction 'final and conclusive', so no court could question it on any ground.
items.detail: The same immunity was given for Article 352 (National Emergency) and Article 356 (President's Rule).

items.what: Deleted this protection. So now courts CAN examine the President's satisfaction (it is open to judicial review).
items.detail: This protection was removed for all three — Article 352, Article 356 and Article 360 — not only for Article 352.

blocks.text: see National Emergency (Art 352) for judicial review of Article 352 and the Minerva Mills case

steps.step: Both Houses of Parliament approve it within two months
steps.detail: Each House passes the approval resolution by a simple majority (a majority of the members present and voting). Remember: two months here; one month is the limit for a National Emergency.

Case 1: Lok Sabha is already dissolved when the proclamation is issued. Case 2: Lok Sabha is dissolved within the two months before approving it. In both cases, the proclamation stays alive until 30 days from the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha — but only if the Rajya Sabha has approved it in the meantime.
There is no maximum period. Parliament does not have to approve it again (no six-month renewal like National Emergency or President's Rule).

steps.step: President revokes it at any time
steps.detail: The President ends it by issuing another proclamation. Ending it does NOT need Parliament's approval.

blocks.title: What the Centre can do
head: Over whom
Power
rows: The Centre can give directions to any state to follow the 'canons of financial propriety' (basic rules for careful and honest use of public money).
The Centre can give any other direction to a state that the President thinks necessary.
Such directions may require the state to reduce the salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving in the state.
Such directions may require the state to send all money bills and other financial bills to the President for consideration, after the state legislature passes them.
The President may direct reduction of salaries and allowances of all or any class of persons serving the Union.
The President may direct reduction of salaries and allowances of judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.
blocks.note: Result: the Centre gets full control over the states in financial matters.

blocks.title: Judges' salaries — the one exception
items: Normally, judges' salaries and allowances cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.
The only exception: during a Financial Emergency. Then the President (not the Chief Justice, not the Prime Minister) can order a cut.

blocks.title: What it does NOT do
items: It does NOT suspend Fundamental Rights. Article 19 is suspended automatically only under Article 358, during a National Emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression.
It does NOT let states cut the salaries of Union (central government) employees. The power flows from the Centre to the states, not the other way.
It does NOT give the President any special power to dismiss the Union Cabinet.

blocks.text: see National Emergency (Art 352) for Articles 358 and 359

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
What he said
rows: Article 360 'more or less follows the pattern' of the National Recovery Act of the United States (1933). That Act gave the US President power to deal with economic difficulties after the Great Depression.
The financial emergency provisions are a serious threat to the financial autonomy (financial independence) of the states.
blocks.note: Do not confuse: the emergency provisions in general are borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany, but Ambedkar linked Article 360 specifically to the US National Recovery Act, 1933.

blocks.title: Use so far
items: No Financial Emergency has ever been declared in India.
Even during the financial crisis of 1991, it was not declared.

head: Control

Centre can direct a state to reduce salaries of persons serving the state
Only during a Financial Emergency — not under President's Rule (Art 356), Article 256 directions, or National Emergency (Art 352)

Governor needs the President's instructions before making an ordinance in certain cases — for example, when a bill with the same provisions would have needed the President's previous sanction (permission) to be introduced
Always — it is a normal provision, not an emergency power
blocks.note: Statement trap: these controls are not limited to Concurrent List matters.

blocks.text: see President's Rule (Art 356, 365)

items: Parliament must approve it within TWO months (not one month).
Each House approves it by a simple majority, not a special majority.
Once approved, it needs no renewal and has no maximum period.
The President can end (revoke) it at any time; this needs no approval from Parliament.
Salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges CAN be cut — on the President's direction.
Fundamental Rights (like Article 19) are NOT suspended by a Financial Emergency.
Never declared, not even in 1991.
Ambedkar said Article 360 follows the US National Recovery Act, 1933. Kunzru said it is a threat to the states' financial autonomy.
